Live from NPR News, I'm Charles Snyder. A commercial flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv
made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia this morning after one of the pilots apparently
stabbed the other pilot and tried to crash the plane with everyone on board. NPR's Kat
Lonsdorf was at the Tel Aviv airport as passengers from that flight finally arrived.
It was a chaotic scene packed with journalists and waiting family members. The passengers
slowly emerged, dragging suitcases, some crying, some smiling, and looking relieved. Some just
looked really tired. There were also quite a few families. Dan Zollert was traveling
with his wife and two small kids and saw much of the incident on board while trying to comfort
his children.
The pilot was stabbed. I don't know who stabbed him, but I know that three passengers threw
themselves on the terrorist and captured him.
Israeli officials are calling it an attempted terrorist attack, but many details are still
unknown. The suspect pilot is in custody, and Saudi officials have begun an investigation.
Kat Lonsdorf, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
Iran says it has received an official response to Tehran's proposal to bring an end to the
seven-month war. Foreign Minister Abbas Araxi presented the response at a cabinet meeting
Wednesday. President Trump rejected that latest offer a few days ago, but Araxi has said that
Iran has not received a formal rejection. Speaking of what he called the State of the
Force address, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth repeated claims that the U.S. military has
destroyed Iran's military capabilities.
Iran's conventional shield has been crippled, and their nuclear ambitions laid bare for
the world. You, this group, are ensuring that Iran never gets a nuclear weapon.
Hegseth spoke Wednesday to junior officers and enlisted leaders at the Marine Corps-based
Quantico in Virginia. He announced some major changes, including establishing a new drone
command and slashing the number of generals and admirals at the Pentagon by 20 percent.
His speech came on the same day that U.S. forces formally withdrew from Iraq after more
than two decades.
Ballots for this year's midterm election in less than five weeks have started going out.
Voters say they have a lot of concerns about mail-in ballots and potential federal interference.
And in Paris, Miles Park's reports turn out still an open question.
Carly Koppes, a Republican who runs voting in Weld County, Colorado, says voters have
a lot of questions right now.
How is this going to work? How are you going to make sure my ballot's going to be counted?
How am I going to get my ballot? I'm hearing all of these things.
It's tempting to think an environment like this might dampen turnout, and midterms already
typically see lower turnout compared to presidential election years.
But political scientists say it's not so simple. In some cases, threats to voting rights can
actually spur higher turnout, as people are extra motivated to vote and political groups
mobilize to respond to the threats.
The highest turnout midterm in modern history was in 2018, during President Trump's first
term.
Miles Parkes, NPR News, Washington.
And you're listening to NPR News.
In Tennessee, lawyers for Christa Gail Pike have filed an emergency motion seeking an
immediate halt to Pike's execution.
Media witnesses say state officials were unable to carry out the execution after administering
two doses of the lethal injection drug.
Earlier in the day, the U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for Pike's execution over
turning a last-minute stay granted by a three-judge appeals court panel.
An NPR investigation finds children with disabilities are the largest group in foster care, and
they have the worst outcomes in foster care.
Here's NPR's Joseph Shapiro.
NPR obtained data on a half million children and youth in foster care.
Our analysis found that disabled kids stay in foster care the longest, 50% longer than
other children.
They're more likely to be moved from place to place.
And they're far more likely to live in institutional settings rather than with a foster family.
Another study found foster kids with physical disabilities are nine times more likely to
die.
Nancy Thaler leads a federally funded program to improve care for kids with tricky behavioral
health issues, kids who sometimes hurt themselves or others.
This is the group that everybody gives up on, and it's because they have disabilities.
But Thaler says new brain science shows these kids can recover and lead successful lives.
Joseph Shapiro, NPR News.
In Europe, experts say Swiss glaciers are shrinking.
But new reports as glaciers in Switzerland have lost more than 5% of their ice volume
due to record heat waves and low winter snowfall.
The report highlights global warming's impact on Europe.
I'm Jael Snyder.
This is NPR News.
